title: Wahe in, guru out
hookLine: many sound Wahe on the in-breath and Guru on the out-breath

cards: Breathing is the one thing you do all day without ever deciding to, and almost none of those breaths get noticed. In, out, while you think about the email, the dishes, the thing somebody said at lunch.
Now put a word on each breath. Not shouted, not even spoken. Just there, like a passenger.
Many Sikhs do exactly this with one word, the word the Sikh code of conduct calls the Gurmantar. They split it in two. The first half rides in.

teach.b: The word is Waheguru. You've met it already on this path: the Gurmantar, the Guru's own word for remembering God. Let's open it.
Wahe is an exclamation of wonder, close to wow, the sound you make when a view stops you on a hill road.
Guru means the teacher, the guide. So Waheguru is something like wonderful Teacher, a cry of wonder at the Divine. Now the breath.
Many Sikhs practice simran by letting Wahe rise on the in-breath and Guru fall on the out-breath. The in-breath is the wonder, taking in. The out-breath is the Guru, letting go into trust.

It's slow, and silent, or nearly so. Some say it quietly on the lips; some only in the mind. Others don't split the word at all, and repeat the whole of Waheguru aloud, in rhythm, or sing it in kirtan with the sangat.
Sikh teachers and groups differ on the details, and the Guru Granth Sahib doesn't lay down a breathing method.
What the hymns do say, over and over, is that a breath without the Name is wasted, and a breath with it is precious. So the breath isn't a trick.
It's a clock you already carry, ticking whether you mean it to or not.
Simran on the breath simply asks that some of those breaths remember where they came from.

how: Many Sikhs practice simran by silently sounding Wahe on the in-breath and Guru on the out-breath; others repeat Waheguru aloud or sing it together in kirtan.

o: a short prayer said before each meal
thinking Wahe, wonder, as you breathe in
holding your breath while you say Guru

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: a cry of wonder, close to wow

s: the Guru Granth Sahib lays down an exact breathing method
it doesn't. the hymns praise remembering with every breath; the method varies among Sikhs.
the Guru's own word for remembering God.
every Sikh splits the word across the breath
many do; others repeat the whole word aloud or sing it in kirtan.

games.q: you're trying wahe in, guru out, and you lose count at breath six. what do you do?
o: start the ten again from one.
just carry on with the next breath.
games.why: the count is only a help. the practice is the next breath with the word on it, whatever number it is.

practice: Sit comfortably and take ten breaths this way: think Wahe slowly through the whole in-breath, and Guru all the way to the end of the out-breath, counting on your fingers if it helps.
If you're here to learn rather than to pray, just listen to how the two halves feel different. After ten, let the words go and keep breathing.

wordCard.voice: Wahe in. The first half of Waheguru, the wonder, riding on the in-breath. Guru rides out.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Waheguru, wonderful Teacher, the Sikh word for God.

carryVoice: Your line: wonder in, trust out. A cry of wonder, then a letting go. That's day one hundred twenty-one.
